newsitem.title: UK: S&P rates Qatar General Petroleum Corp BBB.
newsitem.headline: S&P rates Qatar General Petroleum Corp BBB.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Tuesday it assigned its BBB foreign currency issuer credit rating to Qatar General Petroleum Corporation (QGPC).
This is the first oil company in the Arab world to receive a credit rating from Standard & Poor's, the agency said in a statement.
"The outlook on the rating is stable," S&P said.
S&P said the rating was assigned in connection with Ras Laffan Liquefied Natural Gas Company Ltd's (Ras Laffan) upcoming bond issue.

"The foreign currency credit rating, which is identical to the State of Qatar's, is based on QGPC's close links to the government and strategic importance to the national economy," S&P said. "The stable outlook mirrors that of the State of Qatar, since QGPC's creditstanding is expected to remain linked with that of the government's for the foreseeable future."
S&P said the company's large natural gas reserve base --the world's third largest, modest but growing oil reserves, and strong cash flow, also supported the rating.

"QGPC is wholly state-owned and accounts for two-thirds of government revenues, over 80 percent of Qatar's exports and, excluding its downstream activities, more than a quarter of the country's annual gross domestic product," the agency said.

"As Qatar's only integrated national oil company, QGPC is responsible for all upstream and downstream oil and natural gas operations for the state. Proven oil reserves of 3.7 billion barrels should support over 20 years of output at current production levels. Moreover, new discoveries, being developed under Production Sharing Agreements, could potentially increase reserves by a substantial margin, and should raise QGPC's output in excess of 550,000 bpd by the end of the decade," S&P said.

The agency said QGPC's critical importance to public finances and the real economy would grow as Qatar developed its natural gas resources. Proven gas reserves of 265 trillion cubic feet in the North Gas Field, 12 times Qatar's oil reserves in equivalent billions of barrels, were expected to support 70-100 years of production.

"Liquefied natural gas (LNG) sales, which are scheduled to commence in January 1997, and exceed 10 million tons per annum by 2000, will moderate QGPC's exposure to oil price volatility, and augment and stabilize its revenues as well as those of the government," S&P said.

It said the development of the North Field gas reserves, undertaken by Qatargas LNG Co and Ras Laffan, two joint venture companies in which QGPC is majority shareholder, was expected to cost $7.8 billion over the next three to four years, $5.0 billion of which will be debt-financed.

"As a result, QGPC's financial profile will change significantly, with its debt-to-capital ratio expected to rise to 60-70 percent by 1998 from about 50 percent at present. Although QGPC's close financial links to the government limits the usefulness of a stand-alone financial analysis, cash flow coverage of interest expenses is expected to remain extremely strong, while net income to annual sales will remain well above 10 percent," said S&P.
